beats: Hook: servers used to waste more than half of their most precious memory (the KV cache); the fix came from operating systems (line_paged_turned_away).
Callback: the KV cache is L03-02's cloakroom: each token leaves a name tag (key) and a parcel (value) with the clerk (line_clerk_ladder; line_kv_cloakroom_wall in the library).

The cause (slide 20): nobody knows how long an answer will be, so the old servers reserved one contiguous slab for the maximum length per request (line_paged_reserved_row; car-park version line_paged_carpark_cones).
Waste 1, reservation (slide 20): slots held for future tokens, empty at this step (line_paged_reserved_row).
Waste 2, internal fragmentation (slide 20): the answer ends early, the rest of the slab is never used; her example: reserve 1,000, stop at 100, 900 wasted (line_paged_early_leaver).
Waste 3, external fragmentation (slide 21): gaps between slabs too small for the next request (line_paged_carpark_gaps).
The number (slide 22, taped): more than 50% of allocated KV memory wasted (Orca max / pow2 / oracle), so fewer requests fit at once and decode, being memory-bound, starves (line_paged_turned_away).
The OS idea (slide 23): pages and a page table: logically in order, physically anywhere (line_paged_carpark_bays, line_card_catalog).

PagedAttention (vLLM, SOSP 2023, slides 24-25): small fixed blocks (e.g. 16 tokens; the slide shows 4) allocated on demand; the block table maps logical to physical; at most one partly used block per sequence; any free block fits (line_paged_crates_on_demand, line_paged_ticket_crates).
Sharing (slides 26-27): parallel samples and system prompts reuse the same prefix blocks; copy on write when they diverge (line_paged_shared_coat).

Pitfall (her words): kernels assumed one contiguous slab, so they must follow the block table; the change is 'not that hard'; GPU-friendly block sizes keep the reads coalesced. Next: keep the shared beginnings for later requests (L13-04).

drawings.prompt: A cloakroom seen from the front. Behind a long wooden counter, the clerk (an invented cheerful clerk: simple round face, dot eyes, short tousled hair, a pencil tucked behind one ear, a collared shirt with rolled-up sleeves under a bib apron) holds up one open hand apologetically and shakes the head, turning people away. Behind the clerk, a big wall of open square pigeonholes, about 6 rows by 8 columns: only about one pigeonhole in three holds anything (a small parcel with a blank round name tag); in most of the others stands just a small blank folded card, like a reserved card on a restaurant table, guarding an empty hole. In front of the counter, a queue of four invented guests (simple round faces, dot eyes; different hairstyles: round glasses, a ponytail, a cap, curls, a bob, a bun) with coats over their arms and parcels in their hands look disappointed. Landscape image 1536x1024; the wall and the counter fill about 90% of the width and about 85% of the height. The cards, tags and parcels are blank. No text, no letters, no numbers, no symbols, no logos anywhere.
